posts.title: demo vs production coding agents
posts.hook: We tested our coding agent on a real 40k-line codebase last week. It solved 2 out of 9 tickets cleanly.
posts.body:
We tested our coding agent on a real 40k-line codebase last week. It solved 2 out of 9 tickets cleanly.

Not 2 out of 9 toy problems. 2 out of 9 actual production tickets with legacy dependencies, undocumented API contracts, and migration state that only existed in a Slack thread from 2024.

The other 7? It wrote code that compiled, passed the tests it wrote for itself, and broke three things nobody asked it to touch.

This is the gap nobody talks about in agent benchmarks. The benchmark says 87% pass rate. Your codebase says 22%.

The difference is context. Not model capability. Not prompt engineering. Context.

The agent doesn't know your team renamed that table six months ago. It doesn't know the ORM has a quirk where soft deletes cascade differently than hard deletes. It doesn't know the staging environment has a different auth flow than prod.

So now I spend more time on context engineering than prompt engineering. CLAUDE.md files, structured project docs, MCP servers that expose schema and conventions directly to the agent.

The model is smart enough. The bottleneck is what it knows about your system when it starts working.
posts.cta: What's the ugliest failure you've seen from a coding agent on real code? Not a demo. Real production.

remixes.label: the-context-gap
remixes.hook: Your coding agent doesn't have a skill problem. It has a context problem.
remixes.body:
Your coding agent doesn't have a skill problem. It has a context problem.

We ran the same agent against two codebases last month. One was a greenfield project with clear docs, typed interfaces, and a clean dependency graph. The agent crushed it. 8 out of 10 tasks done, minimal review needed.

The other was a 40k-line monolith. Implicit conventions. Business logic buried in middleware. Migration state that lived in someone's head.

Same agent. Same model. Same prompts. It solved 2 out of 9 tickets.

The difference wasn't intelligence. It was the gap between what the agent could see and what it needed to know.

Every undocumented API contract is a trap. Every implicit naming convention is a landmine. Every piece of tribal knowledge in Slack is a dependency the agent can't resolve.

The teams winning with coding agents right now aren't the ones with the best prompts. They're the ones who invested in making their codebase legible to a machine. README files that actually describe the system. Type contracts that encode business rules. Architecture decision records that explain why, not just what.

Context engineering isn't a nice-to-have. It's the entire unlock.
remixes.cta: What's the biggest piece of tribal knowledge in your codebase that would trip up any new contributor, human or AI?

remixes.label: honest-scorecard
remixes.hook: Everyone shares their coding agent wins. Here's our honest scorecard from last week.
remixes.body:
Everyone shares their coding agent wins. Here's our honest scorecard from last week.

Ticket 1: Add a date filter to the admin table. Agent nailed it. Clean PR, merged in 20 minutes.

Ticket 2: Fix the CSV export encoding bug. Done. It even found a related edge case we missed.

Ticket 3: Refactor the notification service to use the new event bus. It rewired the happy path perfectly and silently broke the retry logic, the dead letter queue, and the rate limiter. Three systems that weren't in the ticket description but were coupled through a shared state object.

Tickets 4 through 9: Variations of ticket 3. Code that compiled. Tests that passed, because the agent wrote the tests to match its own output. Downstream breakage that only surfaced in staging.

The pattern is clear. Agents are excellent at bounded, well-specified tasks. They fall apart when the blast radius extends beyond what's in their context window.

This isn't a reason to stop using them. It's a reason to get precise about what you hand them. Small surface area. Explicit constraints. Clear boundaries.

The 2 out of 9 number isn't a failure. It's a calibration.
remixes.cta: What's your hit rate on agent-generated PRs that actually merge without rework?

posts.title: AI SDRs expose the job
posts.hook: AI SDRs aren't replacing sales reps. They're replacing the part of sales that was already dead.
posts.body:
AI SDRs aren't replacing sales reps. They're replacing the part of sales that was already dead.

The 200-email blast with a merge tag and a prayer. The LinkedIn connect-and-pitch in the same breath. The "just checking in" follow-up sequence that runs for 47 days.

That work was already worthless. AI just does worthless work faster.

The reps who are fine right now are the ones who were already doing the hard stuff. Reading 10-Ks before a call. Noticing a prospect's company just posted three engineering roles (signal: they're building, budget is moving). Threading a cold email through a genuine observation about the prospect's stack.

I built a signal-based outbound system that watches for job postings, funding rounds, and tech stack changes. Enriches through multiple providers, scores by ICP fit, routes to a sequence.

The system handles sourcing and enrichment. A human still writes the angle. Because the angle is the whole game.

If your SDR's entire job was sendable by a sequence tool in 2024, that job was already gone. The AI just made it obvious.
posts.cta: Curious what signals you're actually using to decide who to reach out to and when.

inspired_by.author: Kyle Poyar
inspired_by.summary: AI SDRs are not replacing human SDRs — they're exposing which SDRs were never doing the hard parts. The reps surviving the automation wave are the ones who can run discovery like a consultant, not just book meetings. The job is changing, not disappearing.

remixes.label: automation-mirror
remixes.hook: The fastest way to find out your outbound is broken is to automate it.
remixes.body:
The fastest way to find out your outbound is broken is to automate it.

We plugged an AI SDR into a client's existing playbook last quarter. Same ICP targeting. Same sequences. Same messaging framework. Just faster execution.

Within two weeks the results were obvious. Not obviously good. Obviously revealing.

The open rates were fine. The reply rates were catastrophic. And the client's first reaction was "the AI is bad at writing emails."

It wasn't. The AI was writing exactly the same emails their human SDRs were writing. Same templates. Same value props. Same "I noticed your company recently" openers.

The humans just sent fewer of them, so the bad results were hidden in small sample sizes. At scale, the truth was undeniable. The playbook was broken. Had been for months.

AI SDRs are the best diagnostic tool in sales right now. Not because they're good at selling. Because they're good at exposing what was already failing.

If you plug AI into a broken process, you get a faster broken process. That's actually useful, because now you can see it clearly enough to fix it.

The reps who are thriving right now never relied on volume. They built relationships, read signals, and timed their outreach. AI can't replicate that. But it can free up time for it.
remixes.cta: Has automating any part of your sales process revealed something you didn't want to see?

remixes.label: signal-vs-spam
remixes.hook: There are two types of outbound right now. Signal-based and spam. AI just made the gap wider.
remixes.body:
There are two types of outbound right now. Signal-based and spam. AI just made the gap wider.

Spam outbound: pick an ICP, pull a list, write a sequence, blast it, pray for replies. AI makes this cheaper and faster. It also makes it more ignorable, because now everyone is doing it at the same speed.

Signal-based outbound: monitor job postings, tech stack changes, funding rounds, leadership transitions, content engagement. Reach out when there's a reason. Say something specific about their situation.

The first approach is a volume game that AI won, which means humans lost it. If a machine can do your outbound strategy, your outbound strategy was already commodity.

The second approach is where AI actually helps. Not writing the emails. Surfacing the signals. Monitoring 10,000 accounts for the 15 that are showing buying intent this week. Correlating a VP hire with a tech stack gap with a budget cycle.

The reps who are fine right now aren't the ones who adopted AI SDRs. They're the ones who were already doing signal-based work and now have better signal infrastructure.

AI didn't change what good selling looks like. It just made bad selling impossible to hide.
remixes.cta: What's the most reliable buying signal you actually act on, not just track?

That's not selling. That's data entry with a quota.

And now founders are panicking because a bot can do it for $500/month instead of $65K plus benefits. But the question nobody's asking is: if a bot can fully replicate what your SDR team does, what were you actually paying humans for?

AI didn't kill the SDR role. It killed the theater around it.

The reps who are untouchable right now are the ones who were never playing the volume game. They read earnings calls. They notice when a prospect's competitor launches something. They show up with a point of view, not a pitch.

That's not automatable. But it was also never what most SDR managers were hiring for.

posts.title: replacing a sprint with an agent
posts.hook: Last month I needed an internal dashboard. CRM data, pipeline metrics, content stats. Estimated effort: 2-week sprint.
posts.body:
Last month I needed an internal dashboard. CRM data, pipeline metrics, content stats. Estimated effort: 2-week sprint.

I pointed Claude Code at my Postgres database via MCP, described what I wanted in plain English, and had a working dashboard in 4 hours.

Not a prototype. Not a wireframe. A working app with auth, live queries, and filters.

The catch? It took me two months of groundwork to make that 4-hour build possible.

I had to structure my database with clean schemas. Write CLAUDE.md files that explain conventions. Set up MCP servers so the agent could introspect tables and relationships directly. Build the context layer that makes the agent effective.

This is what people miss when they see these "I replaced a team with AI" posts. You didn't replace the team. You front-loaded the team's knowledge into structured context, then let the agent execute against it.

The 4-hour build was real. But the 2 months of context engineering was the actual work.

If your codebase has no docs, inconsistent naming, and tribal knowledge in Slack... the agent will build you something. It just won't be what you wanted.
posts.cta: What's your ratio of context setup time to agent execution time? Mine keeps trending toward 10:1.

inspired_by.summary: Replaced our entire internal tooling team's sprint with a single Claude Code agent + MCP server connected to our Postgres schema. 11 tools shipped in 4 days. The unlock wasn't the model — it was giving the agent read access to our actual DB so it could self-correct. Thread on what the setup looks like.

remixes.label: iceberg-principle
remixes.hook: Everyone sees the 4-hour dashboard build. Nobody sees the two months underneath it.
remixes.body:
Everyone sees the 4-hour dashboard build. Nobody sees the two months underneath it.

Last month I built an internal dashboard with Claude Code. CRM data, pipeline metrics, content stats. Working app with auth, live queries, and filters. Four hours from prompt to deployment.

But that story is misleading if I stop there.

Here's what the two months before looked like. I structured my Postgres schema so every table has clear relationships and naming conventions. I wrote MCP server configs that expose my database in a way an AI can navigate. I documented my data model in plain English. I built context files that describe what each metric means and how it's calculated.

None of that was "building the dashboard." All of it was required for the dashboard to be buildable in 4 hours.

This is the iceberg principle of AI-assisted development. The visible output is fast and impressive. The invisible foundation is slow, unglamorous, and entirely human.

I see people try to skip straight to the 4-hour build. They point an agent at a messy database with no docs and get frustrated when the output is wrong. The agent isn't the bottleneck. The context layer is.

The real skill isn't prompting. It's building systems that are legible to machines. That's context engineering, and it's the highest-leverage work in software right now.
remixes.cta: What foundational work have you done that made an agent task dramatically easier later?

What I actually did: opened Claude Code, connected it to my Postgres database through MCP, described what I wanted, and iterated for four hours.

What I got: a working app. Not a mockup. Auth, live queries, filters, deployed.

But here's the part that matters for anyone trying to replicate this. My database was already well-structured. My MCP configs were already built. My context files already described the data model. I'd spent two months making my system legible to an AI agent.

The 4-hour build was real. The two-week estimate was also real, for anyone starting from scratch.

The math that matters isn't "4 hours vs 2 weeks." It's "2 months of context engineering plus 4 hours vs 2 weeks." And the context engineering compounds. The next internal tool I build will also take 4 hours, because the foundation is already there.

That's the actual unlock. Not one fast build. A permanently faster build cycle.

posts.title: your CRM stages are fiction
posts.hook: Pulled our pipeline report last Tuesday. $2.1M in Stage 3. Felt great for about 10 minutes.
posts.body:
Pulled our pipeline report last Tuesday. $2.1M in Stage 3. Felt great for about 10 minutes.

Then I checked what Stage 3 actually means. The definition was written in 2023 by someone who left in 2024. It says "technical evaluation in progress." Half the deals in Stage 3 haven't had a call in 6 weeks. One of them the contact left the company.

Your CRM isn't lying to you on purpose. It's lying because nobody maintains the definitions, and reps advance deals to keep their pipeline number up.

So I did something simple. I wrote a script that checks deal stage against actual activity. Last email sent, last meeting booked, last note added. If a deal is in Stage 3+ with zero activity in 21 days, it gets flagged.

Result: $2.1M became $840K of real pipeline.

That's not depressing. That's useful. Now you know what you're actually working with.

The fix isn't better CRM software. It's a 30-line Python script that compares what your stages claim against what actually happened. SQLite, your CRM's API, and a cron job.

Stage definitions are opinions. Activity timestamps are facts.
posts.cta: When's the last time you audited your stage definitions against actual deal activity?

inspired_by.summary: Your CRM is lying to you. Not because anyone lied — because your stage definitions were written by someone who left in 2022. We audited our pipeline last quarter and found 34% of 'Stage 3' deals had never had a second meeting. Fixed the definitions, fixed the forecast. RevOps is data hygiene before it's anything else.

remixes.label: crm-archaeology
remixes.hook: I spent last Friday doing CRM archaeology. Opened 20 deals in Stage 3. Only 6 were actually in technical evaluation.
remixes.body:
I spent last Friday doing CRM archaeology. Opened 20 deals in Stage 3. Only 6 were actually in technical evaluation.

Three had gone dark. Two had champions who changed jobs. One was with a company that got acquired. Four were in early discovery that got optimistically staged up before a board meeting. And four more were legitimate but the contact had shifted to a different stakeholder nobody had logged.

The pipeline report said $2.1M in Stage 3. The reality was closer to $800K, and even that's generous.

This isn't a CRM problem. It's an incentive problem.

Reps get measured on pipeline creation. So deals get staged up. Managers get measured on pipeline coverage. So nobody cleans house. Execs report to the board. So the fiction persists until it shows up as a miss at end of quarter.

The CRM is doing exactly what it was designed to do. It's recording what people tell it. The problem is that what people tell it is shaped by what gets them through the next review cycle.

I've started running monthly pipeline audits with a simple rule. If there's been no meaningful activity in 21 days, the deal gets flagged. Not removed. Flagged. And the rep has to write one sentence explaining why it should stay.

That one sentence requirement has cleaned more pipeline than any automation we've tried.
remixes.cta: What's your threshold for flagging a stale deal? And who actually enforces it?

remixes.label: the-data-trust-crisis
remixes.hook: Your revenue forecast is only as good as the worst data in your CRM. And the worst data is always in the stage fields.
remixes.body:
Your revenue forecast is only as good as the worst data in your CRM. And the worst data is always in the stage fields.

I've audited pipeline for a dozen companies in the last year. The pattern is always the same.

Stage 1 and Stage 2 are reasonably accurate because they're binary. Either there was a meeting or there wasn't. Either they responded or they didn't.

Stage 3 and beyond is where fiction starts. "Technical evaluation" could mean the prospect is actively running a POC. Or it could mean they said "looks interesting, send me some docs" six weeks ago.

The gap between these two realities is where forecast misses live.

The root cause is almost never malice. It's ambiguity. Stage definitions written years ago by someone who left. No clear exit criteria. No required evidence to advance a deal. Just vibes and self-reporting.

The fix isn't more automation. It's fewer stages with harder requirements.

One company I worked with went from 7 stages to 4. Each stage requires a specific artifact. Stage 2 needs a recorded discovery call. Stage 3 needs a signed NDA or POC agreement. Stage 4 needs legal redlines.

Their forecast accuracy went from 62% to 84% in one quarter. Not because the deals got better. Because the data got honest.
remixes.cta: What evidence do you require to advance a deal to the next stage? Or is it still self-reported?

Pulled our pipeline report last Tuesday. $2.1M in Stage 3. Felt great for about 10 minutes.

Then I checked what Stage 3 actually means. The definition was written in 2023 by someone who left in 2024. It says "technical evaluation in progress." Half the deals in Stage 3 haven't had a call in 6 weeks. One of them the contact left the company.

Your CRM isn't lying to you on purpose. It's lying because nobody maintains the definitions, and reps advance deals to keep their pipeline number up.

So I did something simple. I wrote a script that checks deal stage against actual activity. Last email sent, last meeting booked, last note added. If a deal is in Stage 3+ with zero activity in 21 days, it gets flagged.

Result: $2.1M became $840K of real pipeline.

That's not depressing. That's useful. Now you know what you're actually working with.

Stage definitions are opinions. Activity timestamps are facts.

posts.title: 11 days to MVP is the new normal
posts.hook: Shipping an MVP used to take 3 months. Now people are doing it in 11 days with a coding agent as co-pilot.
posts.body:
Shipping an MVP used to take 3 months. Now people are doing it in 11 days with a coding agent as co-pilot.

But here's what actually changed. The coding part was never the bottleneck.

Deciding what to build was. Figuring out who it's for was. Getting the first 10 users to care was.

Claude Code can scaffold a full-stack app in an afternoon. Auth, database, API routes, deployment. That's real. I've done it.

What it can't do is tell you whether anyone wants what you just built.

I've shipped features in hours that took weeks to validate. The build cost collapsed. The learning cost didn't.

So the game changed. Instead of spending 3 months building and 1 month testing... you spend 2 weeks building and 10 weeks testing, iterating, talking to users, and rebuilding.

The founders winning right now aren't the fastest builders. They're the ones who figured out that cheap builds mean you can test more hypotheses per quarter.

5 MVPs in 3 months beats 1 polished product that nobody asked for.

The agent handles the code. You handle the taste.

remixes.label: build-trap-inversion
remixes.hook: Coding agents made building 10x faster. They didn't make deciding what to build any easier. That's the new bottleneck.
remixes.body:
Coding agents made building 10x faster. They didn't make deciding what to build any easier. That's the new bottleneck.

I've watched three founders this quarter scaffold full apps in under two weeks. Auth, database, API, deployment. All working. All launched. All struggling to find their first 10 users.

The bottleneck was never "can I build this." It was always "should I build this" and "for whom."

When building took 3 months, the slow pace forced founders to validate. You'd talk to customers while waiting for the dev cycle. You'd refine positioning because you had time between sprints. The constraint was annoying but it served a function.

Now that function is gone. You can go from idea to deployed app in 11 days. Which means you can also go from bad idea to deployed failure in 11 days.

The founders I see winning right now are the ones who deliberately slow down the decision phase even though they could start building immediately. They spend a week on customer discovery. They validate willingness to pay before writing a line of code. They treat the speed of building as a superpower for iteration, not a shortcut past validation.

Fast building plus slow deciding equals rapid iteration.
Fast building plus fast deciding equals rapid waste.

The tool changed. The discipline didn't.
remixes.cta: How do you force yourself to validate before building now that the build phase is essentially free?

remixes.label: iteration-velocity
remixes.hook: The founders shipping fastest right now aren't building one thing in 11 days. They're building three things and killing two.
remixes.body:
The founders shipping fastest right now aren't building one thing in 11 days. They're building three things and killing two.

That's the actual shift nobody's talking about. Build time collapsing doesn't mean you ship one product faster. It means you can run multiple experiments in the time it used to take to ship one.

I watched a founder last month build three different onboarding flows in a single week using Claude Code. Not wireframes. Working implementations with real user tracking. She put 50 users through each one and killed the two that had drop-off above 40%.

That experiment used to take a quarter. Three sprints of dev time, three rounds of QA, three deploys. Now it's a week.

This changes the math on product decisions. You don't need to be right on the first try anymore. You need to be fast at finding out you're wrong.

The founders stuck in the old model are still agonizing over which feature to build next. Running stakeholder meetings, building consensus, writing specs. By the time they decide, the builder-operators have already tested it, found the problems, and moved on.

Iteration velocity is the new competitive advantage. Not build speed. Iteration speed. The difference matters. Build speed is one direction. Iteration speed includes the kills, the pivots, and the rebuilds.

Your quarterly roadmap should look less like a Gantt chart and more like a hypothesis log.

posts.hook: Stopped writing content that answers existing questions. Started writing content that makes people realize they have a problem.
posts.body:
Stopped writing content that answers existing questions. Started writing content that makes people realize they have a problem.

For months I was doing the standard play. Find the keyword, write the post, capture the search volume. "Best cold email tools 2026" type stuff.

The traffic was fine. The conversions were terrible. Because everyone searching that term is already comparison shopping. You're fighting 40 other listicles.

So I flipped it. Instead of "best cold email tools" I wrote about the actual problem underneath: most outbound fails because you're emailing the wrong people at the wrong time, regardless of the tool.

Then I showed the signal-based workflow. Job change detection --> enrichment --> ICP scoring --> personalized sequence. With the actual schema. The actual logic.

The pattern: find the question your ICP doesn't know to ask yet. Write the answer. Distribute it where practitioners hang out, not where Google sends browsers.

Search captures existing demand. Community content creates it.

remixes.hook: Your best-performing blog post is stealing pipeline from your sales team.
remixes.body:
Your best-performing blog post is stealing pipeline from your sales team.

I had a post ranking #1 for a competitive keyword. 4,000 visits a month. Marketing loved it. Sales hated it.

Every lead from that post came in already committed to a competitor's approach. They were comparison shopping, not problem solving. Our close rate on those leads was under 3%.

So I tried something different. Wrote a post about a workflow problem nobody was Googling yet. No search volume. No keyword strategy. Just a real pattern I kept seeing in sales calls.

That post got 200 visits in its first month. But 11 of those visitors booked calls. Because they read it and thought "wait, that's exactly what's happening to us."

The math changed completely. 200 visits at 5.5% conversion beat 4,000 visits at 0.3% conversion. Every time.

Demand capture content fights over existing intent. Demand creation content manufactures new intent. One has a ceiling set by search volume. The other has a ceiling set by how well you understand problems your buyers haven't articulated yet.

I still write SEO content. But the posts that actually move pipeline are the ones that name a problem before the market does.

remixes.label: tactical-breakdown
remixes.hook: My lowest-traffic post generated more revenue than my top 10 SEO posts combined. Here's the formula I used.
remixes.body:
My lowest-traffic post generated more revenue than my top 10 SEO posts combined. Here's the formula I used.

Step 1: Pull the last 20 sales call transcripts. Ctrl+F for moments where the prospect says "I didn't realize" or "we never thought about it that way." Those phrases mark unrecognized problems.

Step 2: Write about the problem, not the solution. Most content jumps straight to "here's how to fix X." Problem-aware content sits with the pain. It describes the symptoms. It names what's going wrong and why nobody notices.

Step 3: Distribute where your buyer scrolls, not where they search. These posts don't have search volume because the problem doesn't have a keyword yet. LinkedIn, newsletters, communities. Places where people discover instead of seek.

Step 4: Measure differently. Ignore pageviews. Track how many readers mention the post on a sales call. Track how many people DM you saying "this is exactly what we're dealing with."

I published one post like this per week for six weeks. Pipeline from content went from nearly zero to 40% of new opportunities. The traffic numbers looked worse. The revenue numbers looked better than anything I'd shipped from SEO.

posts.title: compute costs falling faster than expected
posts.hook: The cost of running an agentic workflow dropped 60% in the last 8 months. Most teams haven't repriced their roadmaps.
posts.body:
The cost of running an agentic workflow dropped 60% in the last 8 months. Most teams haven't repriced their roadmaps.

I track my agent costs weekly. January: a full research + enrichment + content generation loop cost about $4.20 per run. Today the same loop, better models, runs at $1.60.

This changes what's economically viable to automate.

Six months ago I couldn't justify running an agent loop on every inbound lead. Too expensive at volume. Now I run enrichment, ICP scoring, and personalized first-line generation on every single form fill. $1.60 per lead when leads convert at $15K ACV is a rounding error.

Workflows that were "cool but not worth it" in Q1 are table stakes by Q4.

The teams I'm watching are the ones who re-evaluate their automation boundaries every quarter. What was too expensive to automate 90 days ago might be free now.

My rule: if a workflow touches more than 50 records per week and requires judgment, reprice it monthly. The model economics move faster than your planning cycle.

The question isn't "can we afford to automate this." It's "can we afford to keep doing it manually when the agent costs less than the Slack thread coordinating the handoff."

Six months ago I killed an automation project because the unit economics didn't work. Last week I rebuilt it for 60% less. Nobody told me to revisit it.

I had a lead enrichment workflow. Pull company data, cross-reference tech stack, score fit, generate personalized first lines. Ran great in testing. Cost $4+ per lead in production. At 500 leads a week, that's $2,000/month just on the enrichment layer. Couldn't justify it.

Filed it away. Moved on.

Then I noticed my other agent costs dropping. Checked the math on the old project. Same workflow, current model pricing: $1.60 per lead. That's $800/month instead of $2,000.

The project that was economically dead is now profitable.

This is happening across the stack and most teams aren't going back to revisit killed projects. They made the call six months ago and moved on. But the cost floor moved under them.

I now do a monthly "zombie review." Every project I shelved for cost reasons gets a quick repricing. Two of five zombie projects are now live in production.

If you haven't repriced your shelved AI projects in the last quarter, you're leaving automation on the table that's already economically viable.

AI compute costs are falling faster than teams can update their planning assumptions. That gap is a competitive window.

Most companies set their AI budget in Q4 based on Q3 pricing. By Q2, the actual costs are 40-60% lower than the assumptions baked into the plan. The budget is allocated. The roadmap is set. Nobody goes back to ask "what else could we build with the savings?"

I track my agent costs weekly. Not monthly, not quarterly. Weekly. Because the pricing shifts are happening that fast.

January: my standard research + enrichment + content loop cost $4.20 per run.
March: $3.10.
May: $2.40.
August: $1.60.

Each price drop opened a new category of workflows. At $4.20, I could only justify high-value tasks. At $1.60, I run agents on exploratory work that might not pan out. The hit rate is lower but the cost of experimentation is nearly free.

The teams that reprice monthly are building things their competitors haven't even scoped yet. Because the competitors are still operating on January's cost assumptions.

This window won't last forever. Eventually everyone updates their mental model. Right now, the gap between actual costs and assumed costs is the widest it's been.

posts.title: the career pivot nobody prepared for
posts.hook: I was a plumber for 10 years before I touched a line of code. People act like that's a disadvantage.
posts.body:
I was a plumber for 10 years before I touched a line of code. People act like that's a disadvantage.

Plumbing taught me systems thinking before I knew the term. Water flows downhill. Pressure follows path of least resistance. If you fix the symptom without tracing the pipe back to the source, you'll be back in two weeks.

Same thing in GTM engineering. A sequence that's not converting isn't a copy problem, a targeting problem, or a deliverability problem. It's all three. And they're connected like pipes in a wall. You pull on one, the others move.

The self-taught path gets romanticized. It shouldn't be. It's slow, confusing, and full of mass-produced tutorials that teach you syntax but not systems.

What actually accelerated the transition: building things I needed. Not following a curriculum. I needed a way to track leads, so I built one. Needed to enrich data, so I wired up APIs. Needed outbound infrastructure, so I learned DNS and SMTP.

Every skill was pulled by a real problem, not pushed by a syllabus.

Coding agents made the gap closeable. I don't write code from scratch. I describe systems and validate what comes back. The decade of systems thinking is the asset. The code is the output format.

The best debugging skill I have came from fixing copper pipes under a house, not from a CS degree.

When a pipe leaks, you don't just patch the wet spot. You trace the line back to find where pressure is building, where joints are failing, where the system is stressed. Fix the symptom and you're back under that house in two weeks.

I do the exact same thing with GTM systems now. A sequence isn't converting? That's the wet spot. The real problem might be three steps upstream. Wrong ICP filter. Bad enrichment data. Timing misaligned with the buying signal.

Plumbing also taught me to work in constraints. You can't move a main line. You work around what's already there. Same with enterprise tech stacks. You don't get to redesign the CRM. You build around it.

And the unglamorous work matters most. Nobody posts about cleaning out a drain line. Nobody posts about data hygiene either. But both determine whether the system actually works.

Ten years of plumbing gave me pattern recognition that no bootcamp covers. Pressure, flow, resistance, failure points. Those concepts transfer directly. The people who dismiss trade experience as irrelevant to tech haven't thought carefully about what technical work actually requires.

They were wrong about what counts as zero.

A plumber runs diagnostics on systems every single day. Where is the pressure? Where is the blockage? What's the path of least resistance? You develop an instinct for tracing problems to their source because callbacks cost you money.

Built an outbound system that watches for buying signals instead of blasting lists. 3x reply rate, 80% less volume.

Sent 5,000 cold emails last quarter. Got 12 meetings. This quarter I sent 900 and got 38 meetings. The difference wasn't the copy.

The difference was when I sent them.

Last quarter was the standard spray-and-pray. Big list, decent personalization, send on Tuesday mornings. The ICP filter was "right industry, right company size." That's necessary but not sufficient.

This quarter I added signal triggers. I don't send until something happens. A target account posts a relevant job listing. They raise a round. They adopt a tool in our integration ecosystem. Their competitor just closed a deal with us.

The signal tells me two things. First, the problem is active. They're not going to respond to a cold email about hiring automation if they're not hiring. Second, the timing is right. They're already thinking about this category.

The mechanics: a job posting monitor runs daily against 2,000 target accounts. An enrichment layer adds context. A scoring function ranks signals by recency and relevance. Only accounts above threshold get outreach.

Most days, fewer than 10 accounts qualify. Some days zero. That felt wrong at first. My old brain wanted volume. But 10 well-timed emails outperform 200 generic ones every single time.

The counterintuitive part: doing less outreach takes more engineering. The system to watch, filter, and time costs more to build than a bulk sender. But the output quality isn't even comparable.
remixes.cta: What's the signal that tells you a prospect is ready to hear from you right now?

Here's the exact stack behind my signal-based outbound system. No paid tools except the APIs.

Layer 1: Signal collection. A Python script runs daily, pulling new job postings from target account domains via a job board API. Cost: about $50/month. Also monitors for funding announcements and tech stack changes through a second data provider.

Layer 2: Enrichment. Every signal gets enriched with company context. Employee count, revenue range, tech stack, recent news. This turns a raw signal ("Company X posted a RevOps role") into a qualified signal ("Series B company, 80 employees, uses HubSpot, posted RevOps role after raising $12M").

Layer 3: Scoring. An ICP scoring function weighs signal recency (last 7 days scores highest), company fit (size, industry, tech stack), and signal strength (a VP hire signals more budget than a coordinator role). Only accounts scoring above 75/100 get outreach.

Layer 4: Personalization. The first line references the specific signal. Not "I noticed your company is growing." More like "Saw you're hiring a RevOps manager. Usually means the CRM is getting complex enough that one person needs to own it."

Results after 90 days: 3.2x reply rate compared to bulk outbound. 80% less email volume. Higher average deal size because the timing catches budget holders mid-decision.

Total build time was about two weeks. The ongoing maintenance is maybe an hour per week to tune scoring weights.

posts.title: extended thinking changes agent economics
posts.hook: Extended thinking on Claude costs more per call and saves money overall. Sounds contradictory until you see the loop counts.
posts.body:
Extended thinking on Claude costs more per call and saves money overall. Sounds contradictory until you see the loop counts.

I run agentic workflows that iterate until a task is done. Code generation, testing, fixing, retesting. Each loop costs tokens.

Without extended thinking: the agent makes a quick attempt, gets it 70% right, then spends 4-5 loops debugging and patching. Total: 6 loops, ~$3.20.

With extended thinking: the agent reasons through the problem upfront, gets it 90% right on first attempt, then 1-2 loops to polish. Total: 3 loops, ~$2.40.

The per-call cost went up. The per-task cost went down 25%.

This is the math most teams skip. They see the higher token price and default to the cheaper model. But cheaper per token doesn't mean cheaper per outcome.

I track cost-per-completed-task, not cost-per-API-call. Different metric, different decisions.

Same pattern shows up in GTM. A $0.02 email to 10,000 wrong people costs more than a $2.00 enrichment call on 200 right people. The unit economics only make sense when you measure at the outcome level.

Measure what you're buying, not what you're spending.

Everyone optimizes for cost per API call. The metric that actually matters is cost per completed task. They're often inversely correlated.

I discovered this by accident. I was trying to reduce my agentic workflow costs by using a cheaper model. Cost per call dropped 40%. Total spend went up 25%.

The cheap model needed more loops. It would generate code, miss an edge case, fail the test, patch it, miss another edge case, fail again. Six iterations to do what the expensive model did in two.

Each individual call was cheaper. But six cheap calls cost more than two expensive ones. And the time cost was worse. Six loops meant 3x the latency. What used to take 45 seconds now took 2+ minutes.

Extended thinking made this even more pronounced. Yes, a single extended thinking call costs 3-4x a standard call. But it gets the task right on the first or second attempt instead of the fifth. Two expensive calls beat six cheap ones on cost, speed, and output quality.

The lesson generalizes beyond AI. In most systems, optimizing for unit cost at the expense of completion efficiency makes total cost worse. Cheap components that require rework are more expensive than premium components that work the first time.

I now track three metrics for every agentic workflow: cost per call, loops per task, and cost per completed task. The last one is the only one that matters for budgeting.
